title: Ramadan: the mosque

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramadan at home: a toy of wool, dates at sunset, everyone at the table at once. Today, down the street.

Late one night in Ramadan, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, goes out to the mosque in Madinah and prays. A few men see him and pray behind him. The next night, more people come, and the next, more again, until the mosque is full of people waiting for him. 'A'ishah tells it in Sahih al-Bukhari. Then, one night, he doesn't come out. They wait. He stays home. At the dawn prayer, he explains why.
screen: `HE PRAYS ALONE AT NIGHT.` → `EACH NIGHT, MORE PEOPLE.` → `ONE NIGHT, HE STAYS HOME.`

segments.voice: His explanation, in paraphrase: your being there was not hidden from me, but I was afraid this prayer would be made obligatory on you, and you wouldn't be able to keep it up. He stayed home out of mercy, to keep a voluntary prayer voluntary. The night prayer of Ramadan began as a gift, and he protected it from becoming a burden. Al-Bukhari also reports that later, in the time of 'Umar, he walked into the mosque one Ramadan night and found people praying scattered, some alone, some in small groups behind one man. He gathered them into one congregation behind a single reciter, Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Another night he saw them praying together and said, in paraphrase, what a fine new thing this is. That gathered night prayer came to be called tarawih, which you first met in year one. Schools differ on how long it should be, and not every community prays it in congregation. Shia Muslims, for example, keep Ramadan nights with their own prayers. Before the prayer, the food. In a hadith in al-Tirmidhi, whoever gives a fasting person food to break the fast has a reward like theirs, without the fasting person's reward being reduced at all. So some mosques open their doors at sunset: long sheets on the floor, volunteers carrying trays, dates, water, soup, rice, strangers passing plates to strangers. The family table seats the people who share your house. The mosque table seats whoever walks in: the student far from home, the new neighbor, the person who would otherwise break the fast alone. Ramadan widens the table.
screen: `HE STAYED HOME, OUT OF MERCY.` · `'UMAR GATHERS ONE CONGREGATION.` · `FEED A FASTING PERSON.` · `RAMADAN WIDENS THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: Picture a long cloth on a mosque floor at sunset, plates going down the line, and someone you don't know beside you, passing you a date. Then think whether a mosque near you holds an iftar open to guests, or, if you don't go to a mosque, of one person who eats alone and how you might share a meal. If you pray, you can remember the people who cook and serve.
Ramadan. The month of fasting, kept in the mosque with the night prayer called tarawih and with iftars where whoever walks in gets fed. Today's word.
Your line: the community table. Whoever walks in gets fed. Rest well.

howItsDone: In Ramadan, mosques may hold a congregational night prayer called tarawih, which reports in al-Bukhari trace to 'Umar gathering people behind one reciter, and some host iftars at sunset open to anyone, following a hadith in al-Tirmidhi on the reward of feeding a fasting person; Shia Muslims keep Ramadan nights with their own prayers.
